title: Build a `Map<String, BigDecimal>` of account id to total balance from a stream of transactions where the same account appears multiple times, using `Collectors.toMap` with a merge function. Explain the `IllegalStateException` on duplicate keys and how the merge function resolves it.
shortTitle: Build an account-to-balance map with Collectors.toMap and resolve duplicate keys with a merge function

s1_definition.profdef: `Collectors.toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper)` builds a map from a stream, but throws `IllegalStateException` if two elements produce the same key. The three-argument `toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper, mergeFunction)` resolves collisions by combining the two values, for example summing balances for the same account.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh files each transaction under its account number. If an account already has a slip on file, the two-argument filing clerk panics and stops (IllegalStateException). The three-argument clerk instead adds the new amount to the existing one, so each account ends with its total.
s1_definition.oneliner: `toMap` throws on duplicate keys; add a merge function to combine colliding values, such as `BigDecimal::add` to total per account.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Collectors.toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper)` builds a map from a stream, but throws `IllegalStateException` if two elements produce the same key. The three-argument `toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper, mergeFunction)` resolves collisions by combining the two values, for example summing balances for the same account.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh files each transaction under its account number. If an account already has a slip on file, the two-argument filing clerk panics and stops (IllegalStateException). The three-argument clerk instead adds the new amount to the existing one, so each account ends with its total.

**One line to remember:** `toMap` throws on duplicate keys; add a merge function to combine colliding values, such as `BigDecimal::add` to total per account.

sections.s2_technical:
`toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper)` applies the key mapper and value mapper to each element and inserts them into a map. If two elements map to the same key, it cannot silently overwrite because that would hide data, so it throws `IllegalStateException` with a "Duplicate key" message. This is a deliberate safety default.

When duplicates are expected, the three-argument form `toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper, mergeFunction)` takes a `BinaryOperator` invoked whenever a key collides, receiving the existing and new values and returning the combined result. For balances: `transactions.stream().collect(toMap(Txn::getAccountId, Txn::getAmount, BigDecimal::add))` sums all amounts per account. You can also keep the first with `(a, b) -> a`, the last with `(a, b) -> b`, or the larger with `BigDecimal::max`.

The senior nuance is that the default map is a HashMap; a four-argument overload adds a map supplier, so `toMap(k, v, merge, LinkedHashMap::new)` preserves encounter order or `TreeMap::new` sorts keys. Also, toMap value mappers must not produce null, which throws a NullPointerException, unlike groupingBy. For concurrent accumulation in parallel there is `toConcurrentMap` with the same merge semantics.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes a stream of transactions where each account appears many times, and must produce the net balance per account. A plain toMap would blow up with IllegalStateException the first time an account repeats, which is almost immediately.

This is exactly why the merge-function form of toMap exists — it combines colliding values, so for each repeated account id the amounts are added with BigDecimal::add, yielding the total balance per account.

The code defines a `Txn` record, a `BalanceService.balancesByAccount` method, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: four transactions — SAV2001 for 1000, CUR3001 for 250, SAV2001 for 500, SAV2001 for minus 200.

Step 1: The first SAV2001 transaction inserts key SAV2001 with 1000.

Step 2: CUR3001 inserts a new key with 250, no collision.

Step 3: The second SAV2001 collides; the merge function adds 500 to 1000, giving 1500.

Step 4: The third SAV2001 collides again; the merge adds minus 200, giving 1300.

Step 5: The result is SAV2001 at 1300.00 and CUR3001 at 250.00, each exact in BigDecimal, with insertion order preserved by the LinkedHashMap.

```
INFO: SAV2001 net balance = 1300.00
INFO: CUR3001 net balance = 250.00
```

```
  txns: SAV2001 +1000, CUR3001 +250, SAV2001 +500, SAV2001 -200
    │ toMap(accountId, amount, BigDecimal::add, LinkedHashMap)
    ▼
  SAV2001: 1000 →(+500) 1500 →(-200) 1300.00
  CUR3001: 250.00
    │
    ▼
  {SAV2001=1300.00, CUR3001=250.00}
  (2-arg toMap would throw IllegalStateException at 2nd SAV2001)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Collectors toMap builds a map from a stream using a key mapper and a value mapper, but by design the two-argument form throws an IllegalStateException the moment two elements map to the same key. That default is a safety feature, because silently overwriting would hide one of the colliding values. When duplicates are expected, I use the three-argument form, which adds a merge function — a binary operator that receives the existing and new values and returns the combined result.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I built a net-balance-per-account map from a transaction stream where every account appeared many times. A plain toMap would have failed immediately, so I passed BigDecimal add as the merge function, which summed each account's amounts, including debits as negatives, into an exact net balance, with money kept in BigDecimal throughout.

The senior details I always add are that the merge function can express different rules — sum with add, keep the first with a to b returning a, keep the latest with a to b returning b, or keep the larger with max — and that a four-argument overload lets me choose the map implementation, such as LinkedHashMap to preserve order or TreeMap to sort keys. I also remember that toMap value mappers must not produce null, which throws, and that for parallel accumulation there is toConcurrentMap with the same merge semantics.
